text: k-means makes you commit to k before it starts, and nothing in the data announces the right answer. Pick too few and different customers get lumped together; pick too many and you split natural groups into hair-thin slices nobody can act on. This lesson gives you two standard diagnostics and a third, more important check: does the answer make business sense?

Inertia is the total squared distance from rows to their centroids. Add more centroids and every row can only get closer to one, so inertia decreases as k rises, all the way to zero when k equals the number of rows. You cannot simply pick the k with the lowest inertia — instead you look for the point of diminishing returns.

Sweeping k from 2 to 8 on our illustrative customers and recording both inertia and silhouette score each time: going from k equals 2 to 3 drops inertia from 304.6 to 52.4, a huge improvement. From 3 to 4 the drop is only about 10, and every step after that shaves off even less.
The curve bends sharply at k equals 3, like an elbow, and that bend is your candidate. With messy real data the elbow is often gentle and debatable, which is exactly why we add a second opinion.

The silhouette score compares a point's average distance to its own cluster with its distance to the nearest other cluster, running from negative 1 to 1. Here it peaks at 0.773 for k equals 3, then falls to 0.642 at k equals 4, and down to around 0.51 to 0.53 beyond that. Unlike inertia, silhouette can go down as k rises, so it can name a maximum directly.

Both methods agree on k equals 3 here, which matches the three groups we actually built into the data. Plotting both side by side makes the agreement visible immediately — the elbow and the silhouette peak land on exactly the same k.

Real customer data rarely gives such a clean answer. If the elbow is vague, trust the silhouette; if both are vague, compare candidate values of k by profiling the clusters. Prefer the smaller k when scores are close, since fewer segments are easier to explain and act on.

Ask whether each cluster is large enough to matter and different enough to treat differently — a marketing team that can only run four campaigns is a legitimate constraint on k. Check stability by rerunning with different seeds; if the groups keep changing, they aren't solid. To recap: inertia always falls with k, so look for the elbow; silhouette gives a direct peak; and business usefulness has the final say. Next lesson: hierarchical clustering, which avoids committing to k up front.
